title: Composite function: derivatives and stationary points
statement:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are related (for all real $x$) by
$$g(x)=f(x)+\frac{1}{f(x)}.$$

Express $g'(x)$ and $g''(x)$ in terms of $f(x)$ and its derivatives.

If $f(x)=4+\cos 2x+2\sin x$, find the stationary points of $g$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, and determine which are maxima and which are minima.
solution:
**Part 1.** Using the chain rule,
$$g'(x)=f'(x)-\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)^2}=f'(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{f(x)^2}\right).$$

Differentiating again,
$$g''(x)=f''(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{f(x)^2}\right)+f'(x)\cdot\frac{2f'(x)}{f(x)^3}=f''(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{f(x)^2}\right)+\frac{2f'(x)^2}{f(x)^3}.$$

**Part 2.** With $f(x)=4+\cos 2x+2\sin x$,
$$f'(x)=-2\sin 2x+2\cos x=2\cos x(1-2\sin x).$$

Since $g'(x)=f'(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{f(x)^2}\right)$, and $f(x)\neq 1$ for all $x$ (in fact $f(x)\ge 1$ because $4+\cos 2x+2\sin x\ge 4-1-2=1$), stationary points occur precisely when $f'(x)=0$, i.e.
$$2\cos x(1-2\sin x)=0.$$

Thus either $\cos x=0$, giving $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}$, or $1-2\sin x=0$, giving $\sin x=\frac12$, i.e. $x=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}$.

Evaluate $f$ at these points:
$$f\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=4+\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}+2\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}=4+\tfrac12+1=\tfrac{11}{2},$$
$$f\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=4+\cos\pi+2\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=4-1+2=5,$$
$$f\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=4+\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{3}+2\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{6}=4+\tfrac12+1=\tfrac{11}{2},$$
$$f\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=4+\cos 3\pi+2\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{2}=4-1-2=1.$$

At a stationary point (where $f'(x)=0$),
$$g''(x)=f''(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{f(x)^2}\right),$$
so the sign of $g''$ is the sign of $f''(x)$ (since $1-1/f(x)^2\ge 0$, being zero only at $f(x)=1$, i.e. at $x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$).

Now $f''(x)=-4\cos 2x-2\sin x$:
$$f''\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-4\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}-2\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}=-2-1=-3<0,$$
$$f''\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-4\cos\pi-2\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=4-2=2>0,$$
$$f''\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=-4\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{3}-2\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{6}=-2-1=-3<0.$$

For $x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, $f(x)=1$ so $g''$ is not directly determined by the above; we check directly. At $x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, $f'=0$, $f''=-4\cos 3\pi-2\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{2}=4+2=6$. Since $g(x)=f+1/f$ and $f=1$ here, we can compute $g''(x)=f''(1-1)+2f'^2/f^3=f''\cdot 0 + 0 = 0$ is not decisive; instead note $g(x)=f(x)+1/f(x)$ has a minimum where $f$ itself has $f=1$ (the minimum of $t+1/t$ at $t=1$). Since $f(x)\ge 1$ and $f(\tfrac{3\pi}{2})=1$, this point gives the global minimum of $g$.

Hence:
- $x=\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ are **local maxima**,
- $x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a **local minimum**,
- $x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is the **global minimum** (where $g=2$).
hints: For the stationary points, note g' = f'(1 - 1/f^2) and use f(x) >= 1.
Determine max/min using the sign of g'' = f''(1 - 1/f^2).
